en: The Sūtra on the Incantation for Protecting Bhikṣus Spoken by the Buddha by Seventy-two Thousand Devas of the Consecrated Crown,
Scroll One. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śrīmitra of Central India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard.
At one time, the World-Honored One was traveling among the brahmin villages of Rājagṛha;
from there he traveled north to the Śailagiri mountain, to the Indra Cave.
At that time, countless bhikṣus each fled in haste, restless and uneasy,
like fish caught in a net by a fisherman, scattering in all directions.
The World-Honored One saw from afar that countless bhikṣus were each scattering in all directions, agitated and ill at ease.
Knowing the reason, he nevertheless asked the bhikṣus:
"For what reason do you circle about like this, so unhappy, like fish afraid of a net?"
The bhikṣu replied, "I am tormented by Māra and find no peace anywhere.
By day, I encounter various thieves and robbers, as well as venomous snakes, vipers, and pythons,
and am further harassed by dragons, elephants, bears, and brown bears."
"One cannot attain the fruits of the four paths by means of fixed concentration.
Seeing affliction as such, what should one do?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu, "Do not give rise to distress."
I shall now explain for you the hundred and twenty sovereign deities who follow as your retinue in the consecration chapter;
they shall act as your protectors, warding off evil and ensuring that no harassers or harm-doers find an opportunity to prevail.
Wherever one goes, the protective deities and attendants will grant one auspicious success,
and all malevolent influences will be subdued.
The bhikṣus rejoiced upon hearing what the Buddha had spoken.
With his mind opened and his understanding clarified, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
I pray that you will expound the verses of empowerment."
Protect us and all the bhikṣus of future ages, granting them peace and security,
and causing them to enter into the practice of meditative concentration.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now, for your sake, clearly and individually explain the one hundred and seventy-two names of the great kṣetrapāla kings of the consecration chapter."
"Listen thus with careful attention and mindfulness; do not forget it.
The bhikṣus replied, "Yes," and accepting the instruction, they joined their palms and listened silently to the Buddha's words.

The deity is named Daoke-mi-jialuo-yixili; the deity is named Xili-yinpi-eroluobi; the deity is named Mobiqiu-pilaidouhulai-sha; the deity is named Shijuli-yintile-biqupipi; the deity is named Oulasumizhelu-erluoyin; the deity is named Aluoye-agipozhe; the deity is named Yewuzhadi-piyie-abi; the deity is named Ona-she-ta-omiti-tu. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "These are the eighteen divine kings."
He protected the bhikṣus and the bhikṣus of future ages,
as well as the saṃghārāma.
The Buddha saw that the group of bhikṣus on Mount Piṇḍava were in a state of hurried agitation and unease.
By day they are harassed by thieves and evil persons;
by night they are beset by ghosts and spirits,
as well as terrified by dragons, elephants, bears, brown bears, tigers, and wolves.
Furthermore, having been afflicted by the poison of *gū* (sorcery),
the Buddha then extensively expounded for the assembly of bhikṣus these unsurpassed mantras of consecration and the names of the great spirits and deities.
May all bhikṣus always obtain the blessings of peace, security, and auspiciousness, free from all calamities and harms.

There is a deity named Śarī, a deity named Mahāśarī, a deity named Śarāṇī, a deity named Ukka-mukka, a deity named Sappati, a deity named Acchivechi, a deity named Nacchi-kunacchi-panate, a deity named Tevasa-rāpate, and a deity named Anāpate-panate. Thus the Buddha told the bhikṣus.
These twelve spirit kings protect the bhikṣus and others;
neither devas nor ghosts, whether human or non-human, dare to harass or approach them.
Poisons do not take effect, and they are not burned by fire or swept away by water.
Local officials and thieves shall find no opportunity to cause harm;
enemies and creditors shall be unable to plunder [one's property].
The divine kings and their retinues, along with seven hundred followers, shall constantly provide protection, expel all malevolent forces, and ensure that all matters are auspicious.

The deity named Kāhaṇī Mahākāhaṇī; the deity named Akhani Khani Akhana; the deity named Akhanī Abilamandara; the deity named Padanī Pāṭaligā. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "These are the ten divine kings."
I shall protect the bhikṣus of the present and future ages,
so that they are not harmed by the five types of pestilential poisons,
nor possessed by cruel spirits.
When the names of these ten divine kings are invoked, the cruel spirits will retreat and disperse.
You should protect yourself and likewise speak of this for others so that they may obtain the merit of auspiciousness.

The names of the divine kings are: Mahā-ruruka-ri-khu-hve; Kin-yen-ta-yueh; A-nou-san-p’u; Chia-li-sien-mo; Mo-ho-a-shu; Po-to-sha-lo-man-t’o-lo-a; Chia-na-kuo-she; Ho-ho-lo-lo; Sha-sha-t’o-t’o; Mo-mo-chia-chia; Po-to-sha-lo-man-t’o-lo-lo; and Hu-hu-i-i-ye-ye-ho-ho. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “These are the sixteen divine kings.”
Together with his retinue of fifteen thousand spirits, he shall protect all bhikṣus of the present and future ages.
In the past, the bhikṣu Uruvilvā was harassed by eighty-one billion māras.
By reciting the names of these sixteen spirit-kings,
all the retinues of Māras will be overturned and fall;
they will crawl away in disarray.
Its physical forms undergo transformations such that it cannot be hidden.
[The Buddha] told the bhikṣus: "If there should be days of peril, distress, or terror, by invoking the name of this deity, one will immediately obtain auspiciousness."
May all the deities provide protection and assistance, driving away all malevolent forces.

The name of the deity is Āpajje-jñapti-jñapti-mudrā; the name of the deity is He-che-pi-che-zhan-po-zhan; the name of the deity is Bakāra-huṅ-anuśu-anu; the name of the deity is Jhu-anu-tai-la-song-he-lo; the name of the deity is Chen-lin-ra-pā-ya-vyāla-ra; the name of the deity is Dantira-sāra-kha-ya-dha. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "These are the sixteen divine kings."
Together with his retinue of five thousand followers,
each by means of their own majestic spiritual power,
cleared away the malevolent transformations of ghosts and spirits for the sake of the bhikṣus.
In the past, my son Rāhula was practicing meditation beneath a tree when he was harassed by malevolent spirits.
Startled, he rose and came to me the following day.
I then spoke, saying, "I shall now recite for you the incantations to expel ghosts and spirits.
I then recited these names of the sixteen divine kings.
The Buddha said to Rāhula: "If among the fourfold assembly of disciples..."
For those who are being tormented by ghosts and spirits,
one should recite for them these sixteen divine kings’ consecration mantras,
so that they may be freed from all calamities and attain the blessings of auspiciousness.

The deity is named Ārāyakiṃpila; the deity is named Pañcika; the deity is named Haripiṅgala; the deity is named Maṇibhadra; the deity is named Sahaka; the deity is named Dharmarāja-kānta; the deity is named Kumāra; the deity is named Sumakānta; the deity is named Gopaka; the deity is named Cañca; and the deity is named Cāṭa. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "These twelve great deities are the heroes among all ghosts."
Together with his retinue of thirty-five thousand,
he fought against the various devas; at that time, he suppressed the rākṣasas who,
having formerly not known the Dharma, took blood as their food.
They constantly devour people, small children, and their like;
now, having been taught the Dharma by me, they have all attained the Way and made a great vow:
"In the future, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the age of the five turbidities and chaos..."
They protect the assembly of bhikṣu disciples and cause them to obtain the merit of auspiciousness.

The names of the deities are: Śarī and Mahāśarī; Śalānī and Utpalā-mukhī; Sarpadattā and Mahāsarpadattā; Atrapadattā and Kujjhitā; Sarabhadattā and Anubhadattā; Panabhadattā and Janabhadattā; Kaccānī and Mahākaccānī; and Pāsāṇadevī and Khemiyā. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "These are the nineteen spirit-kings."
In another land, in a world-system named Flower Accumulation (Puṣpasaṃcaya),
there is a Buddha named Supreme Heavenly King Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
He has dispatched two bodhisattvas.
The first is named Immeasurable Radiance, and the second is Great Radiance.
These two bodhisattvas dispatched these nineteen divine kings and their spirit-mantras, speaking thus:
"All the people of the Sahā world..."
Those who practice good are few, while those who commit evil are many.
Therefore, we offer these nineteen spirit-kings to assist the World-Honored One,
so that all sentient beings may be tamed and inspired with faith and understanding.
Now, for your sakes, I shall proclaim those nineteen divine incantation-kings offered by that Buddha;
these thirty-six thousand spirits and ghosts constitute their retinue.
I shall provide for you all various forms of protection,
deliver you from calamities and suffering so that you may attain auspiciousness and universally enter the Dharma-gate.

The deity named Kāṭalīlimālani; the deity named Kālarāmudiroli; the deity named Ālīcibenduliyi; the deity named Mālīcī-Akacchiyi; the deity named Nantīyī-Ana-nuoluoqi; the deity named Pūṭala-zi-Jūlarala-zi; the deity named Nakalī-zi-Būṭala-zi; the deity named Jūlan-zi-Duoluo-zi; the deity named Būṭaṭala-zi-Jūla-zi; the deity named Duojali-li-momalanini; the deity named Jūlan-mīṭala-jūliti; the deity named Kasira-munidieuli; the deity named Kalaninlidicapei. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "These are the twenty-seven divine kings."
In the past, when the bhikṣu Huatí was repairing and protecting his dwelling,
a black snake emerged from between the walls and bit him.
Huatí immediately fainted and fell to the ground.
Ānanda immediately went to where the Buddha was and inquired about this matter.
The Buddha then replied to Ānanda:
"Tell Mahādeva this."
I shall explain for him the transformation of the body through the protection of the twenty-seven divine kings who dispel snake venom;
I shall say to Huatì: "You should maintain a heart of compassion and take pity upon the myriad insects of the world."
"Recite these words of mine and your poison shall be extinguished.
Ānanda immediately sprinkled divine water upon Cūḍapanthaka,
and Cūḍapanthaka was awakened to realization.
Ānanda then spoke to Cīrṇadhvaja, saying:
"The Buddha has already taught you the method for the twenty-seven spirit-kings to dispel snake venom.
You need only maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward all people in the world, and the poisons of both humans and non-humans will naturally be extinguished."
Ānanda then recited for Huatī the twenty-seven royal spirit-mantra methods taught by the Buddha;
Huatī was immediately healed.
Ānanda said to the bhikṣus:
"If there is a place where one dwells in peace and security,
one should speak these words."
A snake’s venom will not bite anyone again for seven years.
By reciting these divine names twenty-one times, one immediately attains auspiciousness.

The names of the deities are: the deity Antaniṣadamaṇi, the deity Jamani, the deity Mahānīla, and the deity Mūkarāṭṭhi-cakrapadmavibhu. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "These are the twelve divine kings."
In the past, the Buddha spoke of this deity’s name for the sake of the bhikṣu Kana.
There was a wicked and cruel man who constantly robbed the bhikṣu of his robes.
The bhikṣu went to the Buddha’s presence and reported this matter to him.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu: "If, while you are practicing the twelve dhūtas in the mountains, under trees, or among burial mounds,
there are wicked people who come to harass you,"
"You should now recite the names of these twelve spirit-kings;
then malevolent persons will naturally retreat and disperse,
departing by another path and unable to cause harm."
One may practice dhyāna to seek the fruits of the four paths, attaining the auspicious merit of being free from all calamities and hardships.
The spirits are named Āṭavaka, Aṭaṭaka, Pañcika, Kūṭadanta, Pārana, Kūṭavera, Pālāla, Śarabha, Pārṣṇika, Dantaputra, and Sumati. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "These are the twelve spirit kings."
In the past, there was a bhikṣu named Prajñātīva who,
while reciting and studying the various sūtras and dharmas, suffered from cold and wind,
and consequently had his teeth gnawed by worms.
I have spoken these phrases for the sake of this bhikṣu and for all disciples in future ages.
If there should be bhikṣus or members of the fourfold assembly whose teeth are gnawed by insects, [they should recite them].
Using a vessel of pure water, take a mouthful of water and hold your teeth above it;
recite these names of the twelve spirit-kings seven times,
then spit out the water held in your mouth.
If this rite is performed forty-nine times in this manner,
the worms will immediately break apart and scatter, rushing away with the flowing water until none remain;
one will then obtain the auspicious merit of recovery.
The deity is named Eliphu; the deity is named Ilabifu; the deity is named Uhani-mohalai-lou-lou; the deity is named Daogeshaliyana; the deity is named Jiliduosengpomuna. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
In the past, there was a bhikṣu named Guṇata who suffered from wind-induced eye pain.
He also suffered from unbearable itching and pain caused by moisture-worms.
He came to my place and reported these matters to me in detail for inquiry.
I shall then recite for them this divine mantra so that the six kings may provide protection.
If there are bhikṣus or faithful laymen and women in the final age whose eyes are being gnawed by worms, [they shall be protected].
"You should recite these six divine mantras for them;
there shall be no failure to achieve recovery, and there will be the auspicious merit of well-being.
The Buddha addressed the fourfold assembly, including the bhikṣus and others.
In the past, there was a bhikṣu named Shanke who dwelt among the mountains,
practicing dhyāna beneath a tree.
When the time approached, he put on his robes, took up his alms bowl,
and entered the city and villages to wander for alms.
At that time, there was an evil Māra who had eighty-four thousand minor spirits as his retinue.
He met with Śāṇakavāsin.
Māra thought to himself: "This śramaṇa Śāṇakavāsin has attained arhatship and is thus able to deliver himself."
Thinking thus, having conceived a mind of jealousy with the intent to further instruct all other people and cause them to enter the state of arhatship,
he then commanded his minor demonic hordes to come forth.
As for that which is wholesome entering directly from the mouth into the belly:
it may disturb the wholesome and cause the mind to become inverted, so that one cannot attain right mindfulness.
Yet, even so, the wholesome person has already attained arhatship.
Within his heart, he naturally attained a vast and lucid understanding and immediately gained mindfulness.
At that time, the Buddha had previously, for the sake of the bhikṣus,
expounded the hundred and seventy-two mantras of consecration for the divine kings.
Having recollected this, he immediately snapped his fingers;
with single-minded concentration, he recited and chanted aloud,
whereupon the evil Māra and his retinue retreated, dispersed, and fled.
The ranks of his retinue and attendants do not know where he dwells.

The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: "I shall now, for your sake and for the sake of all bhikṣus in future ages, extensively expound the names of the one hundred and seventy-two spirit-kings of consecration."
These divine kings, together with their retinues of seventy-two thousand spirits and ghosts,
shall each protect you all by means of their own majestic power,
ensuring that minor māras find no opportunity against you.
Wherever one goes, there shall be no obstruction;
it will expel and ward off evil serpents, vipers, and adders,
as well as various beasts such as elephants, dragons, bears, and brown bears.
They shall naturally perish, and none shall dare to oppose them.
If there are spirits or deities who come and go and do not depart,
the Four Heavenly Kings shall dispatch their messengers.
Holding the vajra-pestle, he shattered his head into seven pieces.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu, "This great chapter is most true and most sublime.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time have fully expounded this great chapter."
I, too, shall open this precious casket and bring forth these verses.
If there be any bhikṣu who wears and carries them,
whatever place he travels to, virtuous deities will provide him with protection and assistance.
It banishes all evils so that demons dare not confront it;
should any malicious intent arise, it shall naturally perish.
This great divine scripture is to be worn and carried by those who possess it.
Just as a king wearing his sword ensures that plotters do not dare to confront him,
so too is this Great Divine Scripture: for those who wear and carry it,
the various evil māras from without [shall likewise be unable to approach].
Furthermore, the māras of the five aggregates within his body were all subdued.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words,
Ānanda was standing on his right side.
Then, having adjusted his robes and prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, he knelt on his right knee and addressed the Buddha,
saying, "World-Honored One,
for the sake of the bhikṣus, the Tathāgata..."
I have spoken these seventy-two thousand mantras for the consecration of the deities.
In a future age when the Dharma is about to perish,
if there should be anyone who receives these great mantras, how should they be bestowed?
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "This great and divine scripture is most supreme and most weighty.
The Tathāgatas do not proclaim it in vain, nor do they bestow it upon others.
If there is one who upholds the precepts and does not transgress the prohibitions,"
Those who protect and mind all sentient beings of the ten directions;
those who open the intent of the Mahāyāna to deliver suffering beings;
and those who, having approached spiritual friends, hear and accept [the teaching] without slandering it.
"To such a person who seeks it with single-minded devotion, you should grant it.
Ānanda again joined his palms and addressed the Buddha,
saying, "How should it be granted?"
The Buddha said: "If there are those who receive this protective scripture for the body, they should first pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions;
next, pay homage to the Jewel of the Sūtra; and finally, pay homage to the Noble Saṃgha."
Next, pay homage to the teachers of the Vinaya-piṭaka.
All should concentrate their minds with single-minded devotion,
baring the right shoulder, kneeling for a long time, and joining their palms.
The Master shall hold the text in his right hand,
while the disciple receives it with his right hand.
The Master then holds the ritual water (dharmodaka) in his left hand and pours it over the crown of the disciple’s head.
Ānanda, for these reasons it is called the "Mantra of Consecration.
Why is this so? It is because when a crown prince succeeds to the royal throne, according to the law, water should be poured upon his head.
Thereafter, my Dharma for governing the state is likewise.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "If there be a bhikṣu who delights in receiving this scripture, he should suspend five-colored banners and canopies forty-nine feet in length."
Scatter flowers of the five directions, each according to the color of its respective quarter;
burn sandalwood incense, frankincense, bdellium, and so forth;
observe the precepts with single-minded devotion and abstain from the five pungent roots.
One must not drink alcohol or eat putrid meat.
One must not consume any substances that are greasy, such as clarified butter, curd, ghee, or various oily foods.
First, one should bathe the body and don fresh, clean garments.
On a high mountain, smear the ground with fragrant liquid over an area seven feet in length and breadth; this is called a *maṇḍala*.
Upon this, one should transmit these twelve divisions of the subtle and wondrous scriptures of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
On the day you receive [the precepts], you should contemplate the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and noble Saṃgha of the ten directions.
With sincere devotion, pay homage to them and to the master who transmits the sutras;
do not think of matters concerning the east, west, south, or north.
For example, a bhikṣu engaged in meditative contemplation has no other thoughts;
only by guarding a single dharma does he subsequently perceive the truth.
If there is a bhikṣu who receives the sūtras and their chapters and phrases in this manner without distraction, [he likewise perceives the truth].
Seventy-two thousand spirits and deities followed him in front and behind,
providing protection for his person and protection for the deity,
and were likewise able to provide protection for others.
Evil and wicked influences were expelled, and the myriad poisons could not prevail.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "At the time I spoke these words, several li to the west of the city of Rājagṛha, there was a great golden mountain."
Among them were many bhikṣus who had cultivated the fruits of the four paths;
upon hearing this recitation of the consecration verses,
they all adjusted their robes and came to where I was.
Having prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, he sat to one side to listen to the exposition of the Dharma.
At that time, there was among the assembly a young bhikṣu who had already attained arhatship, named Bhūta.
Rising from his seat, he stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.
Kneeling with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you have expounded the unsurpassed, true, and wondrous Dharma."
Regarding these twelve sections of the sublime scriptures on the mantras of empowerment,
I shall, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
widely proclaim and disseminate this profound and wondrous canon.
If there should be a land that encounters calamities and misfortunes,
where officials issue summonses and ten thousand diseases spread,
I shall recite this sutra therein.
All hundred poisons and myriad evils shall be dispersed and eliminated.
Having spoken these words, one should immediately recite and propagate them,
preaching these wondrous scriptures of the twelve divisions.
In this manner, it was successively transmitted to the various bhikṣus, each of whom was instructed to propagate it,
so that throughout all lands this scripture was fully obtained.
When that bhikṣu reached the time of his death,
During the remaining twenty-one days of the third seven-day period, he reflected within his own mind:
"Regarding the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s teachings, these consecrated phrases and subtle, secret, and wondrous scriptures,
during the three hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa..."
And this sutra shall then disappear and no longer be manifest.
Why is this? Because at the very beginning after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who practice goodness will be many, while those who do evil will be few.
In the final age, during the nine hundred years [following the Buddha's passing],
the path of Māra will flourish and various followers of external paths will appropriate the Buddha’s sublime sūtras as their own.
He instructed the myriad people, commanding them to receive and uphold [the teachings].
Furthermore, he made a solemn oath to transform and conceal the methods of the sutras.
On the day they were to receive them, everyone used precious jewels.
Various multicolored silks were used as a token of trust,
after which [the object] was bestowed.
At that time of year, the various kingdoms were waging war against one another.
The people were largely in a state of desolation and chaos; they valued food, drink, and martial prowess.
There were many thieves and bandits, and half of the population died violent deaths.
Furthermore, various evil kings eradicated the Triple Gem, causing the words of the Dharma to be obstructed from circulating.
When stupas are destroyed and the Sangha is extinguished, the Three Jewels gradually decline.
Although the kings of the Central Kingdom may possess faith,
they are unable to exercise ultimate restraint over many matters.
Their minds will not be single-minded, and they will be deluded by heterodox paths.
At that time, there shall appear in the world a bhikṣu named Pujie (Universal Salvation),
who will dwell within stone chambers on various famous mountains, meditating with focused concentration.
Thus, traveling on and on, he came upon a fine cave chamber.
There he saw a precious casket, which he opened and examined;
within it, he found this title of the sutra written in purple and gold.
Having seen this [scripture] carved upon sandalwood tablets,
this bhikṣu joined his palms with single-minded devotion,
prostrated himself with his head at the ground, and recited, upheld, and practiced it.
When such sublime scriptures and the Buddha-dharma have perished,
and after a thousand years have passed, the calamities and transformations will be as follows.
[At that time,] the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and noble Saṃgha...
The devas, nāgas, and all eight classes of supernatural beings,
as well as all ghosts and spirits, seeing these calamities and portents,
take pity on sentient beings who will undergo various sufferings and afflictions during the final age.
May this bhikṣu appear in the world to rescue and deliver sentient beings from peril, distress, and suffering,
so that they do not fall victim to the nine untimely deaths.
By means of this sutra, may the fourfold assembly— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—
and all sons and daughters of good family in future generations, read, recite, propagate, and teach it.
May they obtain auspicious blessings.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "After my passing, the Dharma teachings will become thin and diluted.
Although you may be diligent and disregard all toil and hardship,"
For the sake of all disciples of the fourfold assembly,

he expounded the subtle and unsurpassed Sūtra of the Great Chapter of Consecration spoken by the infinite Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions— the twelve divisions of the sublime scriptures, the secret treasury of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Having already expounded it,
I desire that this sutra circulate throughout the world,
so that those who have not yet heard it may all come to know and see it.
Those who have various doubts and have not yet resolved their uncertainty regarding the Dharma shall have their minds opened and their intentions clarified, attaining great benefit and peace.
Furthermore, Ānanda, I have spoken this sutra.
During the first hundred years after his initial parinirvāṇa,
there were many bhikṣus who could recite and master the teachings,
and those who propagated them were likewise very numerous.
When [the lifespan] reaches two hundred years, many among the fourfold assembly of disciples will attain the Way.
By the time it reaches three hundred years, this sutra and its Dharma will no longer have any utility;
for this reason, they will vanish and cease to appear in the world.
Therefore, it is said that those who do good will mostly not commit great evils.

This profound and wondrous divine scripture is upheld by Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, the world-protecting benevolent deities, and the dragon kings of the mountains and rivers; it contains the twelve divisions of sūtras and the mantras of consecration.
The divine texts shall be contained within a casket of the seven precious gems and placed inside a stone chamber-cave;
in the future, at the end of the age, there will be bhikṣus who practice dhūta austerities.
While wandering through the mountains in search of a suitable meditation cell,
he encountered this sutra; upon opening it and reading it,
he paid homage with palms joined and received it upon the crown of his head.
He proclaimed it far and wide so that all might hear and know; yet,
once this great chapter of the sūtra text had appeared, few were those who accepted it,
while many practiced slander and refused to believe or receive it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the final age, although there may be faithful laymen and faithful laywomen who receive and uphold the Three Refuges and the precepts of the Fivefold Law within my Dharma,"

Failing to understand that suffering, emptiness, and the four great elements are not the self, they constantly cling to the notion of a self; through such inverted discrimination, they give rise to various false views.
When the day of illness arrives, they are tormented by calamities.

he sought life but could not find it, and sought death but could not find it.
A host of spirits and deities then seized the elder, preventing him from moving.
The Buddha, seeing this, felt compassion for him and thought of him.
He then asked the elder, "What will you do now?
The elder’s mouth was clenched, and he could no longer speak.
He could only raise his hands and beat his own chest.
He beseeched the Buddha for mercy, repenting his evil deeds and returning to the good.
The Buddha then used his majestic spiritual power to deliver the elder.
When the various kṣetrapāla kings saw that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had used his majestic supernatural power to rescue the elder,
they each stood to one side.
Thereupon, the elder recovered slightly.
He immediately rose, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: "Within my own body there are these five thieves who drag me into the three evil realms."
"Sitting here, I have committed offenses and have violated what I have received.
I pray that the Buddha will take pity on me and accept my repentance.
The Buddha said to him:

"Who should be held accountable for what has been done by my own mind and speech? The householder addressed the Buddha, saying, "From this day forward, I shall reform my past ways and cultivate myself for the future;
I accept the Three Refuges and the precepts of the Fivefold Discipline."
I shall observe the six fasts of the month and the three long fasts of the year,
burning incense, scattering flowers, and hanging various banners and canopies to serve and honor the Triple Gem.
From this day forward, I dare not again violate or break the laws of the precepts.
The Buddha said, "What you have just said is most excellent.
That which your eyes see and your body experiences is created by oneself and obtained by oneself; it is not bestowed by a heavenly deity."
The Buddha said to the elder, "Now you shall receive these Three Refuges and Five Precepts.
Do not again follow the former method of receiving the refuges and precepts;
to violate these refuges and precepts is called a second offense."
If one commits the three offenses, they will fall into the hands of the Five Officials.
Furthermore, they will fall into the hands of the minor attendants of the King, the Director of Records, and the Surveillance Officers of the Five Emperors’ messengers.
Their spirits shall be seized and their lives recorded, all according to their original crimes.
For this reason, I have spoken these words:
to encourage faithful laymen and laywomen to receive the precepts of refuge.
There are thirty-six kings of ghosts and spirits who will follow them and provide protection and assistance.
The Precepts have twenty-five deities who guard the left and right doorways, expelling the wicked and malevolent.
They are the deities of the Return to the Precepts sent by the Heavenly Emperor from above the Six Heavens.
There shall be as many as billions upon billions, like the sands of the Ganges;
the various kings of the ghost spirits will take turns in succession to protect them, ensuring they do not decline or waste away.
All the devas will rejoice and say, "Excellent! We shall together protect them."
If one maintains the precepts in such a way that they are complete and perfect,
the immeasurable Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats currently residing throughout the ten directions will all join in praising them.
When such a layman or laywoman of pure faith approaches the time of their death, [the Buddhas will appear before them].
The Buddha manifests emanations of his body to go forth and welcome them,
so as not to allow men or women who uphold the precepts to fall into the evil realms.
If their observance of the precepts is weak, they should further cultivate merit and virtue.
One should practice generosity, uphold the precepts, cultivate patience, exert diligence, maintain single-minded concentration, and develop wisdom;
one should light lamps, burn incense, scatter flowers of various colors,
hang silk banners and canopies, and offer praise through song, while paying homage with reverence and prostration.
Furthermore, by maintaining the fasts and precepts, one may also attain transcendence.
If one is unable to cultivate such meritorious virtues as described above,
yet maintains the precepts imperfectly while seeking blessings and protection from various heterodox paths, [one will not escape].
The ghost kings and spirits, as numerous as the sands of billions of Ganges Rivers, each departed from the three refuges and the five precepts.
Malevolent ghosts frequently came to harass those nearby;
because of this affliction, they brought disease and disorder to their households.
Various illnesses and pains arise, leading ultimately to death and ruin;
wealth cannot be accumulated, and whatever one undertakes meets with failure.
After death, one falls back again into the midst of hell.
Although one may be fully endowed with the precepts, if one does not observe the six fast days,
it is like a flowering tree that bears no fruit, a woman who does not give birth,
or sown grain that does not flourish— there will be no profit from one's livelihood.
The capital was lost through waste and embezzlement, and the officials were left without robes or hats;
because they did not observe the precepts of fasting, their profit was such as this.
The Buddha said, "O Householder!"
If a person violates what they have received and thus breaks their precepts,
they will fall under the control of two hundred and seventy divine kings of the heavens;
they will no longer be beyond the reach of external māras.
These spirits observe the goodness and evil of people.
If one upholds the prohibitions and precepts without transgression,
they open the person's mind and reveal their good and evil.
If a person is unwholesome, they shall be subjected to harm; their good and evil deeds are recorded in detail and reported to the Great King.
The Great King, holding these records, inflicts punishment according to the gravity of the offense, treating them with legal severity for the duration of their life so that no resentment remains.
He caused those who had broken the precepts to accept it with a willing heart.
The Buddha told the brahmin,
"The elder has firmly maintained his resolve and abandoned that heterodox path."
Within my Dharma, they have received and upheld the precepts of taking refuge,
yet their minds are unstable and they further violate them;
consequently, they provide an opening for ghosts and spirits to exploit them, causing them to undergo various sufferings and pains.
Now, repenting and reproaching myself, I seek compassion and offer this confession;
I shall reform and cultivate goodness, performing all manner of meritorious deeds to extinguish all evil dharmas, so that now all may attain the Way.
Within the entire family, including all members and the extended clan,
they saw that the elders upheld the retribution of sins and blessings,
and that everyone received from them the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
By steadfastly refraining from transgressions, all shall attain the purity of the Dharma-eye. Now, within this assembly,
I shall extensively explain the karmic causes and conditions of the elder’s past lives, clarifying the evidence of sin and merit.
To ensure that it may be widely proclaimed and circulated for future generations so that all may hear and know it,
the Buddha said to the brahmin: "If there are faithful laymen or faithful laywomen who have been seized by malevolent spirits or evil ghosts..."
If one is suddenly seized by government officials,
robbed by thieves,
or encounters days of great illness and calamity;
When bathing the body,
the man shall wear a single-layered garment and white socks, while the woman shall wear plain garments;
they shall then rinse their mouths and cleanse their teeth.
For seven days and seven nights, they observed the long fast and ate only vegetarian food.
They prepared a fine, high seat, hung silk banners and canopies,
sprinkled fragrant water upon the ground, and burned sandalwood incense.
If one recites and praises this great chapter of empowerment seven times a day,
this wondrous scripture, the true secret treasury,
will eliminate all immeasurable calamities and transformations.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O God among Gods, you have already been able to explain for me and for all sentient beings of the ten directions the Three Refuges,
the Five Precepts, and the names of the ghosts and spirits."
If a man or woman wishes to receive it, how should it be conferred?
The Buddha said: "If a person wishes to receive it, they should first pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Kneeling with palms joined, they should speak as follows:"
"I, disciple [Name], for as long as life lasts, receive the three refuges and the five precepts.
May all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, true persons, and noble assemblies take pity on us.
The Brahmin asked again: "Is there a distinction between receiving the refuges and receiving the precepts?"
The Buddha said: "There is no distinction.
If a person receives [the precepts], one should first set forth the dharma of the Three Refuges and Five Precepts;
thereafter, the names of the spirit-kings should be appended beneath the refuges and precepts."
Write the names of these spirit-kings on fine white silk;
wear them as you go about.
You should burn incense and pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
One should observe the fast for seven days on the eighth day of the month.
When traveling or moving about, one should always wear it upon the body—
either upon the crown of the head or upon the chest.
If one encounters evil Māras, none will not be dispelled.
When men or women invoke the names of these benevolent deities of the Three Refuges and Five Precepts,
if they enter a shrine of spirits, all those malevolent deities will startle and rise up to pay homage to that person.
Why is this? Because this person wears and maintains the names of the deities associated with the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts taught by all Buddhas.
The Buddha said to the brahmin:
"The names of these refuges, precepts, and deities are most supreme and most weighty."
"The Buddhas protect and sustain you; you should propagate and practice this well.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, Ānanda rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said to him:
"How should this Dharma teaching be named?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "This sutra is named 'The Sutra of the Consecration Chapter, the Return to Precepts, and the Wearing of the Amulet.
" Having spoken thus, the Buddha [concluded].
The fourfold assembly, the people, the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of supernatural beings, and all spirits were filled with great joy;
they paid homage and respectfully practiced [the teaching].

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śrīmitra of Central India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Great Monastery in the kingdom of Rājagṛha.
There were one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples, each residing in separate chambers.
The Buddha was alone in his room, reflecting to himself:
"After my parinirvāṇa, the fourfold assembly of disciples will not be fully observant of the precepts; they will transgress them in many ways."
They will commit unrighteous acts and fail to practice the ten wholesome paths.
Once my Dharma has perished, during the final age,
ghosts and demons will arise in confusion, performing all manner of evil deeds to harass and afflict the people.
Furthermore, there was a venomous dragon that spat poison to harm people.
Having thought, "How shall I drive it away? he remained silent.
Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of Devas, knew what the Buddha was thinking.
Rising from his seat, in the time it takes a person to bend and extend their arm,
he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
and having completed his salutation, knelt with palms joined.
The petitioner previously addressed the Buddha, saying: "I pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for the salvation of sentient beings,
will proclaim the names of the Great King of Mantras, the Supreme Consecration Chapter,
for the purpose of protecting the myriad people."
May they be brought to peace and security, freed from all perils and calamities, and delivered from evil.
May no demons or malevolent spirits be able to cause them harm,
and may the names of the deities who have made vows always remain by their side.
"To protect people from evil and prevent poison from taking effect, you have made such a request; I pray that you will expound it.
The Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively and receive this well."
I shall now expound it for you,
so that all sentient beings in the world who take the three refuges may do so.
By fully reciting and upholding the names of these one hundred great deity-kings,
one shall protect the human body and ward off evil and malevolence,
ensuring that the myriad poisons do not prevail and that the people live in peace and security.
Billions of deities and spirits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges shall all be unable to remain;
even those spirits whose names are worn upon one’s person, or those ghosts and spirits dwelling within the body, shall not depart from it.
"The Four Heavenly Kings shall dispatch messengers who will take vajra-wrenches and shatter their heads into seven pieces. Śakra,
Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Dharma praised by the World-Honored One is subtle and wondrous.
I pray that you will expound it to transform those who have not yet heard it.
The Buddha said to Śakra, "This is the *Abhiṣeka-mantra-sūtra*, a dhāraṇī for making vows."
It is profoundly deep and subtle, and cannot be spoken of recklessly.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not recklessly proclaim or bestow it upon others.
Now that I have appeared in the world, I encounter the five evils.
If I do not preach this Sūtra of the Vow-Mantra,
various malevolent minor spirits will come to harass people one after another,
seeking food and drink from them and looking for their faults.
I shall now expound this for you and for all people.
The Buddha spoke to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
"There are one hundred kings of spirits who currently dwell upon the summit of Mount Sumeru."
By my majestic spiritual power, I have summoned their messengers and personally commanded the divine kings to protect you all,
ensuring that you do not encounter untimely calamities; I have bound threads and called upon their names.
"These kings of spirits shall always remain at your side to provide you with protection.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked, "What are their names?
The Buddha said:

The deity named Elimiṭi, titled Unobstructed Virtue; the deity named Niūchūzhē, titled Great Abandonment of Self; the deity named Bōluónátóu, titled Roaming in Peace; the deity named Wúhuóchālóu, titled Returning to Right Transformation; the deity named Sàduōbōluó, titled Delivering from Calamity; the deity named Xīmóhétóu, titled Radiant Illumination; the deity named Tiānlóumójù, titled Proclaiming the Teachings; the deity named Āluóhuòjū, titled Opening the Way to Clarity; and the deity named Náluónáiyí, titled Accordance with Others—these nine divine kings shall, by means of their majestic spiritual power, act as guardians for [Name], warding off the malevolent and evil, so that there may be no afflictions or calamities.
Other ghosts and spirits shall find no opportunity against him;
for a distance of one hundred yojanas, none shall harass or harm him.
This is because he wears and maintains the names of these spirit-kings while making a vow.
All external evil māras shall be eliminated without exception. One shall obtain wholesome benefits and peace, and be granted auspiciousness.

The name of the deity is Maheśvara; his title is the Sovereign God of Majestic Spirit. The name of the deity is Maṇibhadra; his title is the God of Majestic Subduing Conduct. The name of the deity is Pūrṇabhadra; his title is the God of Accumulated Sincerity. The name of the deity is Kiṃpila; his title is the God of Majestic Royal Likeness. The name of the deity is Citrasena; his title is the God Who Knows Reverent Excellence. The name of the deity is Piṇḍola-bharadvāja; his title is the God Established in Immovability. The name of the deity is Carpaṭa; his title is the God Liberated through the Virtue of Patience. These seven divine kings, by means of their own majestic power, [shall protect you].
Together protect [Name] and eliminate all inauspiciousness:
the ill-omened cries of birds, evil dreams, and the strange transformations of wild beasts—
may those who cause calamity and affliction to people be unable to harm [Name].
Because one wears [this] and holds the names of these deities while making vows, one obtains such blessings as these:

The deity named Dharmapāla (曇摩拔羅), whose title is King of Learning; The deity named Makarapāla (摩竭波羅), whose title is Remover of Crookedness; The deity named Śūramitra (繡利密多), whose title is One of Meritorious Achievement; The deity named Rāṣṭrapāla (勒那翅奢), whose title is Harmonizer and Pacifier; The deity named Lambasadevi (斂摩舍帝), whose title is Subduer of All Faculties; The deity named Śarabhidevi (奢羅密帝), whose title is Joyful in Solitude; The deity named Himavat (醯摩拔陀), whose title is Attaining What is Contemplated. These seven divine kings shall, by the power of their majestic spiritual authority, provide protection for [me, the practitioner].
If one enters rivers, seas, lakes, ponds, streams, or valleys,
and there are among the waters various venomous creatures such as *mākaras* and *nāgas* who harbor malicious intent, when wind and waves arise—
By wearing this amulet and invoking the name of the deity who binds vows,
one will naturally attain peace and security, safely crossing over all calamities;
wherever one goes, one shall find tranquility, auspiciousness, and reach the further shore.

The deity named Satākī, whose epithet is Great Power; the deity named Pārirāhu, whose epithet is Valiant Progress; the deity named Vemacitra, whose epithet is Lofty Resonance; the deity named Śyāmali-putra, whose epithet is Heroic Virtue; the deity named Pārila-putra, whose epithet is Flourishing Martial Splendor; the deity named Khara-karṇa, whose epithet is Roaring Like Thunder; and the deity named Kaurava-danti, whose epithet is Unconquerable in Battle—these seven divine kings shall, by means of their majestic virtue, provide protection wherever they are required.
If one enters among the assemblies of those who follow heterodox paths and their food is tainted by poison or the influence of sorcery,
upon consuming that food, it will naturally digest and the poison will not take effect.
By the power of these spirit-kings who wear and uphold their vows, one shall obtain such blessings and retributions in the present life as follows:

The spirit named Hagi-luo-huan (Andhaka), styled "Firmly Immovable"; The spirit named Mo-ni-po-lo (Maṇiprabha), styled "Flowing Eloquence"; The spirit named A-po-ti-lo (Abhyudgata), styled "Joyful Fearlessness"; The spirit named Tan-wu-li-lo (Dharmarāja), styled "Resplendent Adornment"; The spirit named Jian-tuo-ni-xu (Kāntanīkṣu), styled "Firmly Abiding"; The spirit named Qu-mo-he-lo (Gomahara), styled "Pure Radiance"; The spirit named Mo-ha-sha-li (Mahāśrī), styled "Transcending All Difficulties. These seven spirit-kings, by means of their majestic spiritual power, shall act as protectors for [the name of the person].
If there are enemies who, with poisonous and evil hearts, envy the virtuous and the capable,
or who quarrel over wealth and treasures, harboring resentment and engaging in incessant strife,
these seven divine kings will immediately use their majestic power to resolve the conflict between the two families.
May they bring about reconciliation so that wholesome minds arise together and all evil intentions are extinguished.
Such are the immediate rewards for wearing and carrying the names of these spirit-kings (*devaputra*) tied as cords:

The spirit named *Jñānāli*, whose epithet is "Whose Splendor is Virtuous"; The spirit named *Kīroṣṇu*, whose epithet is "Attaining Success in Undertakings"; The spirit named *Lekkaśailu*, whose epithet is "Eliminating Afflictions"; The spirit named *Mācatālī*, whose epithet is "Filling the Celestial Ranks"; The spirit named *Rāmanuñca*, whose epithet is "Opening the Right Path"; The spirit named *Kaṅkaluñca*, whose epithet is "Strength Firmly Established"; The spirit named *Āriluhuang*, whose epithet is "Departing from All Destinies. These seven spirit-kings shall assist you on your left and right with their majestic spiritual power.
In their livelihood and trade, they always obtain double the profit.
They are not led astray by enemies, thieves, or evil companions.
Wherever they travel, all who see them rejoice.
Facing one another with harmonious joy and without any expression of anger or vexation, they manifest such immediate retribution because they bear and uphold the names of these divine kings.

The name of the first deity is *Yuan-naluo-che* (Aṇāla), meaning "Remover of Fear. The name of the second deity is *Weisheluo-che* (Viśāla), meaning "Transcender of Difficulties. The name of the third deity is *Yingjiatuo-luo* (Aṅgadāra), meaning "Enveloper of Heaven and Earth. The name of the fourth deity is *Zheluoluo-jia* (Cakravāka), meaning "Self-Intrepid. The name of the fifth deity is *Tuntouli-jia* (Dundubhika), meaning "Virtue Like a Mountain. The name of the sixth deity is *Naweishi-ni* (Navīśanī), meaning "Thought Without Attachment. The name of the seventh deity is *Tuoyoutuo-luo* (Dhyutāra), meaning "Abiding in Fearlessness. These seven divine kings shall, by means of their majestic spiritual power, provide protection for [the petitioner].
It dispels the dangers and calamities of official authorities;

Punishments such as the cangue, shackles, fetters, and the scourge of the staff are likewise eliminated.
Insults, verbal abuse, spittle, and vomit shall be immediately removed and dissolved. Such present retribution occurs by the power of wearing and upholding the names of these deities.

The deity named Pūjādhara, whose title is "Victorious Banner Suspended"; The deity named Śaravara, whose title is "Vast Holy Speech"; The deity named Narahama, whose title is "Bestower of the Inexhaustible"; The deity named Hevasama, whose title is "Leading Tranquility"; The deity named Acamūra, whose title is "Awakening to Impermanence"; The deity named Piccayya, whose title is "Discriminating Understanding"; The deity named Ciravahi, whose title is "Excellently Exhorting Auspiciousness. These seven spirit-kings, through their majestic spiritual power, shall preside over those who give birth.
By the power of binding and upholding the name of this deity and making vows, other malevolent spirits and ghosts shall not obstruct the birth canal;

When there is no pain or affliction, the child will be born easily;

By wearing and binding this knotted thread, one obtains such blessings as these.

The name of the deity is Śamārudhi; his title is Unrivaled Fulfillment. The name of the deity is Śukhāvatī; his title is Celestial Majesty. The name of the deity is Akṣobhyani; his title is Incomparable Eloquence. The name of the deity is Vīramati; his title is Beyond Doubt. The name of the deity is Sughosamaya; his title is Subduer of Lesser Māras. The name of the deity is Timaruci; his title is Liberator from Birth and Death. He presides over the various minor malevolent dragons within the five warm seas and mountains;

which oppress the myriad people so that they suffer from headaches.
